label: Landmark Judgments & Legal GK
blurb: The constitutional canon plus the legal vocabulary the paper assumes you already have. Cases ranked by how often they actually appear.

topics.title: Kesavananda Bharati (1973) and the amendment cases before it
topics.hook: Thirteen judges, sixty-eight days of hearing, eleven separate opinions and a 7-6 split that decided Parliament can amend the Constitution but cannot rewrite what it is.
topics.story:
The line of amendment cases runs in five steps and the exam expects all of them.

**Shankari Prasad (1951).** Challenge to the First Amendment, which had added the Ninth Schedule. Held that "law" in Article 13 does not include a constitutional amendment, so Fundamental Rights could be amended.

**Sajjan Singh (1965).** Reaffirmed Shankari Prasad by 3-2. Justices Hidayatullah and Mudholkar doubted it, and Mudholkar first floated the idea of "basic features".

**Golaknath (1967).** An eleven-judge bench reversed course 6-5. Chief Justice Subba Rao held that an amendment is "law" under Article 13 and Parliament cannot abridge Fundamental Rights at all. He applied prospective overruling so earlier amendments survived.

Parliament answered with the **24th Amendment (1971)**, declaring that Article 368 amendments are not "law" for Article 13; the **25th Amendment (1971)**, inserting Article 31C; and the **29th Amendment**, putting Kerala land reform laws into the Ninth Schedule.

**Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973).** Swami Kesavananda Bharati, head of the Edneer Mutt in Kasaragod, challenged Kerala land reform laws. The bench of thirteen was assembled to decide the amendment question. Judgment came on **24 April 1973**. By 7-6 the Court overruled Golaknath, upheld the 24th Amendment, and held that the amending power does not extend to altering the **basic structure** of the Constitution. Chief Justice S.M. Sikri retired the following day. The second part of Article 31C, barring judicial review of laws claiming to implement Directive Principles, was struck down.

**Minerva Mills (1980).** Chief Justice Y.V. Chandrachud struck down clauses 4 and 5 of Article 368 and read down the expanded Article 31C, holding that the balance between Parts III and IV is itself a basic feature. Justice Bhagwati partly dissented.

**I.R. Coelho (2007).** Nine judges held that laws inserted into the Ninth Schedule after 24 April 1973 are open to challenge if they damage the basic structure. The Ninth Schedule stopped being a safe harbour.

facts.v: Swami Kesavananda Bharati, head of the Edneer Mutt, Kasaragod
S.M. Sikri, who retired the next day

facts.k: Case that first hinted at basic features

topics.why: The chain of five cases is the single most examined sequence in Indian constitutional law. Learn which case overruled which, and the 7-6 split.

topics.title: SR Bommai v Union of India and Article 356
topics.hook: The Supreme Court restricted the arbitrary use of Article 356 by the central government, establishing federalism and secularism as basic features.
topics.story:
The SR Bommai judgement (1994) is the defining ruling on Article 356 of the Constitution of India, which allows the imposition of President's Rule in states. The case arose after the dismissal of the Janata Dal government in Karnataka led by S.R. Bommai in 1989. The Governor dismissed the government without giving Bommai a chance to prove his majority on the floor of the assembly. Several other state governments were also dismissed around this time, leading to a consolidated batch of petitions before a nine-judge bench of the Supreme Court.

The Court held that the power of the President to dismiss a state government is not absolute. It is subject to judicial review. If the Court finds that the dismissal was based on irrelevant or mala fide grounds, it can strike down the Presidential proclamation. The Court's detailed guidelines mandated that the President can only suspend the assembly upon issuing the proclamation, and dissolution can only occur after parliamentary approval. This procedural safeguard prevented the Centre from presenting a fait accompli to Parliament. Importantly, the Court ruled that the floor of the assembly is the only place to test a majority, stopping the practice of Governors deciding a Chief Minister's strength based on subjective reports.

The judgement also classified federalism and secularism as part of the basic structure of the Constitution. A state government acting against secularism can be dismissed, as happened to four BJP state governments after the demolition of the Babri Masjid in 1992. The Court upheld those dismissals while invalidating others.

Before Bommai, Article 356 was frequently misused to topple opposition governments. Since 1994, the frequency of President's Rule has dropped significantly. The ruling shifted power back to elected state assemblies and made the floor test an unskippable requirement for proving confidence.

facts.v: S.R. Bommai v. Union of India

topics.why: CLAT usually tests the relationship between the Centre and states. The examiner will likely focus on the basic structure additions (secularism) or the floor test principle.

topics.title: Maneka Gandhi (1978) and the golden triangle
topics.hook: A passport impounded "in the public interest" without reasons, and the judgment that turned Article 21 from a formality into the most powerful provision in the Constitution.
topics.story:
In July 1977 the government impounded Maneka Gandhi's passport under section 10(3)(c) of the Passports Act 1967 "in the interests of the general public", and declined to give reasons. She moved the Supreme Court under Article 32, arguing breaches of Articles 14, 19 and 21.

A **seven-judge bench** decided in January 1978. The holdings that matter:

**Articles 14, 19 and 21 are not watertight compartments.** *A.K. Gopalan* (1950) had held that a law depriving personal liberty need only satisfy Article 21, and that Article 19 had no application. Maneka Gandhi overruled that approach. A law must now survive all three, which is why the three are called the **golden triangle**.

**"Procedure established by law" means fair procedure.** The procedure must be right, just and fair, and not arbitrary, fanciful or oppressive. American due process was thus read into a text that had deliberately avoided it.

**Natural justice is implied.** Even where a statute is silent, the audi alteram partem rule applies unless expressly excluded. The government's refusal to give reasons failed this test.

**The right to travel abroad is part of personal liberty**, following *Satwant Singh Sawhney* (1967).

The Court did not quash the order. The Attorney General gave an undertaking that the petitioner would be given a hearing and reasons, and the Court disposed of the petition on that basis. The doctrine outlived the outcome.

Everything expansive in Article 21 since 1978 rests on this case: livelihood in *Olga Tellis*, a clean environment in the *M.C. Mehta* line, legal aid in *Hussainara Khatoon*, speedy trial, shelter, health, privacy in *Puttaswamy* and dignity in death in *Common Cause*. Read with *E.P. Royappa* (1974), it also cemented arbitrariness as an independent ground under Article 14.

facts.v: Procedure must be right, just and fair
Right to travel abroad as part of personal liberty

topics.why: Any passage where the State restricts a freedom without giving reasons is a Maneka Gandhi question. The examiner usually wants the golden triangle named, or the shift from Gopalan.

topics.title: Mohd. Ahmed Khan v Shah Bano Begum and Muslim Personal Law
topics.hook: The Supreme Court upheld a divorced Muslim woman's right to maintenance under Section 125 of the CrPC, sparking a political backlash and legislative override.
topics.story:
In 1932, Shah Bano married Mohd. Ahmed Khan. Decades later, Khan divorced her and refused to pay regular maintenance. Shah Bano filed a petition under Section 125 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, which compels men to maintain their wives, children, and parents if they are unable to maintain themselves. Khan argued that under Muslim personal law, his obligation ended with the iddat period (roughly three months).

A five-judge Supreme Court bench ruled in 1985 that Section 125 is a secular provision. It applies to all citizens regardless of their religion. The Court held that if there is a conflict between personal law and Section 125, the secular criminal law prevails. The judgement affirmed Shah Bano's right to maintenance beyond the iddat period, citing the Quran to state that providing for a divorced wife is a religious duty as well. The judges argued that true religion cannot conflict with social justice.

The ruling caused a massive uproar among orthodox Muslim groups who saw it as interference in personal laws. The Rajiv Gandhi government, holding a massive majority in Parliament, bowed to the conservative backlash. They passed the Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Divorce) Act, 1986. This law essentially nullified the Supreme Court judgement by restricting a divorced Muslim woman's right to maintenance from her former husband to the iddat period alone. The burden of maintenance was shifted to her relatives or the Wakf Board.

The political capitulation remains a debated episode in Indian history, often cited as a failure to enact a Uniform Civil Code under Article 44. Subsequent judgements, like Danial Latifi (2001), have reinterpreted the 1986 Act to require a husband to make a fair provision for the entire future within the iddat period, practically reviving the Shah Bano principle.

facts.v: Section 125 is secular and applies to all religions
Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Divorce) Act, 1986
Danial Latifi v. Union of India (2001)

topics.why: The conflict between secular criminal law and personal law is a regular CLAT theme. Questions often target the 1986 Act and the political aftermath.

topics.title: Shayara Bano v Union of India and the End of Triple Talaq
topics.hook: A five-judge bench struck down the practice of instant triple talaq (talaq-e-biddat) as unconstitutional and arbitrary.
topics.story:
Shayara Bano was married for 15 years before her husband divorced her by pronouncing 'talaq' three times in a letter. She challenged the practice of talaq-e-biddat (instant triple talaq), polygamy, and nikah halala in the Supreme Court. The Court decided to focus solely on talaq-e-biddat, leaving the issues of polygamy and nikah halala for future consideration. They formed a five-judge multi-faith bench to hear the matter.

In a 3:2 majority ruling in 2017, the Court declared instant triple talaq unconstitutional. The reasoning varied among the majority judges. Justices Rohinton Nariman and U.U. Lalit held that the practice is manifestly arbitrary and violates Article 14 (right to equality). They noted that the practice allows a man to break marital ties whimsically and capriciously, without any attempt at reconciliation. Justice Kurian Joseph concurred in the outcome but reasoned that instant triple talaq lacks legal sanction in Islamic theology itself, meaning it is not protected by personal law.

Chief Justice J.S. Khehar and Justice S. Abdul Nazeer dissented. They argued that personal laws are protected under Article 25 (freedom of religion) and cannot be tested against fundamental rights. They directed the Parliament to frame a law instead.

Following the judgement, the Union government passed the Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Marriage) Act, 2019. This law criminalised the pronouncement of instant triple talaq, making it a cognizable and non-bailable offence carrying a jail term of up to three years. The criminalisation of a civil wrong remains a matter of legal debate, with critics arguing that jailing the husband defeats the purpose of securing maintenance for the wife.

facts.v: Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Marriage) Act, 2019

topics.why: Passages usually focus on the concept of 'manifest arbitrariness' introduced by Justice Nariman or the debate around criminalising a civil wrong.

topics.title: Vishaka v State of Rajasthan and Workplace Harassment Guidelines
topics.hook: In the absence of legislation, the Supreme Court laid down binding guidelines to prevent and redress sexual harassment of women at the workplace.
topics.story:
The Vishaka case arose from the brutal gang-rape of Bhanwari Devi, a social worker in Rajasthan who was trying to stop child marriages as part of a government programme. The trial court acquitted the accused, prompting outrage. Several women's rights groups filed public interest litigations in the Supreme Court, highlighting the complete absence of laws to protect working women from harassment.

In 1997, the Supreme Court acknowledged that sexual harassment at the workplace violates the fundamental rights to equality (Article 14), life and liberty (Article 21), and the right to practice any profession (Article 19(1)(g)). Recognising the legislative vacuum, the Court used its powers under Article 141 and Article 32 to lay down the 'Vishaka Guidelines'. The Court explicitly drew upon international conventions, particularly the Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination Against Women (CEDAW), to interpret the fundamental rights, noting that international treaties can be read into domestic law if they do not conflict with it.

The guidelines defined sexual harassment broadly, covering physical contact, demands for sexual favours, sexually coloured remarks, and any other unwelcome physical, verbal, or non-verbal conduct of a sexual nature. They made it mandatory for employers to provide a safe working environment and required the establishment of an Internal Complaints Committee (ICC) in workplaces, headed by a woman and including an external member, to hear grievances.

These judicially created guidelines functioned as law for 16 years. In 2013, the Parliament finally enacted the Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace (Prevention, Prohibition and Redressal) Act (POSH Act), which codified and expanded upon the Vishaka Guidelines.
topics.why: The use of international treaties to interpret domestic fundamental rights is a regular exam topic. The structure of the ICC under the POSH Act is also frequently tested.

topics.title: KS Puttaswamy v Union of India and the Right to Privacy
topics.hook: A unanimous nine-judge bench ruled that the right to privacy is an intrinsic part of the right to life and personal liberty under Article 21.
topics.story:
The challenge to the Aadhaar project led to one of the most significant constitutional rulings in Indian history. When petitioners argued that mandatory biometric collection for Aadhaar violated the right to privacy, the Union government claimed that the Constitution does not guarantee any fundamental right to privacy, relying on older judgements like MP Sharma (1954) and Kharak Singh (1962). To resolve this, a nine-judge bench was formed.

In August 2017, the Supreme Court unanimously declared that privacy is a fundamental right. It is protected as an intrinsic part of the right to life and personal liberty under Article 21, and as a part of the freedoms guaranteed by Part III of the Constitution. The judgement expressly overruled the earlier decisions in MP Sharma and Kharak Singh. It encompasses spatial privacy, decisional autonomy, and informational privacy.

The Court clarified that the right to privacy is not absolute. Any restriction on privacy by the State must pass a three-pronged test: it must be backed by a valid law, pursue a legitimate state aim, and be proportionate to the objective sought. This proportionality test has since become the standard for assessing state intrusions into personal liberties.

The Puttaswamy judgement shifted Indian jurisprudence. By establishing privacy as a fundamental right, it laid the groundwork for subsequent rulings, including the decriminalisation of homosexuality in Navtej Singh Johar (2018) and the striking down of the adultery law in Joseph Shine (2018). It also forced the government to draft comprehensive data protection legislation, eventually resulting in the Digital Personal Data Protection Act of 2023.

facts.v: Aadhaar challenge leading to privacy ruling

topics.why: It is the bedrock of modern fundamental rights jurisprudence in India. The proportionality test and the cases it overruled are prime material for MCQs.

topics.title: The statutes a legal GK paper assumes you know
topics.hook: Most legal GK questions are not about cases. They are about which Act covers what, and how many days you have.
topics.story:
**Right to Information Act, 2005.** Any citizen may request information from a public authority, which must reply within **30 days**, or **48 hours** where life or liberty is involved. The machinery is a Public Information Officer in each authority, an appeal to a first appellate authority, and a second appeal to the **Central or State Information Commission**. Section 8 lists the exemptions: sovereignty, foreign relations, commercial confidence, cabinet papers, and personal information with no public interest. The **2019 amendment** let the Centre fix the tenure and salary of Information Commissioners, which had previously been set in the statute, and the **DPDP Act 2023** widened the personal information exemption.

**Consumer Protection Act, 2019**, which replaced the 1986 Act. It created the **Central Consumer Protection Authority**, brought **e-commerce** and misleading advertisement within its reach, made **product liability** a statutory claim, introduced mediation, and allowed a complaint to be filed where the complainant resides. The three-tier commissions are **District** up to ₹50 lakh, **State** to ₹2 crore, and **National** above that; appeals run upward and then to the Supreme Court. A complaint must ordinarily be filed within **two years**.

**Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act, 2012.** Gender-neutral, applies to anyone below **18**, and reverses the usual burden: **Section 29** presumes the accused guilty once foundational facts are proved, and **Section 30** presumes a culpable mental state. It requires child-friendly procedure, recording of the statement by a woman officer at the child's residence where possible, in-camera trial, and completion within **one year**. The **2019 amendment** added the death penalty for aggravated penetrative assault.

**Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005** is civil, not criminal. It gives a right to reside in the shared household, and provides protection, residence, monetary, custody and compensation orders through a Magistrate, with a Protection Officer to assist. Violation of a protection order is the only criminal offence in it.

Also standing: the **Maintenance and Welfare of Parents and Senior Citizens Act 2007**, the **Motor Vehicles (Amendment) Act 2019** which raised penalties sharply, the **Juvenile Justice Act 2015** allowing 16 to 18 year olds to be tried as adults for heinous offences after a Board assessment, and the **Mental Healthcare Act 2017**, which decriminalised attempted suicide in effect and created advance directives.

facts.v: Reply in 30 days, or 48 hours where life or liberty is at stake; Section 8 exemptions
Tenure and salary of Information Commissioners moved from statute to executive rule
Replaced the 1986 Act; created the CCPA; covers e-commerce and product liability
District to ₹50 lakh, State to ₹2 crore, National above
Applies below 18; gender-neutral; Sections 29 and 30 reverse the burden
Civil in nature; right to reside in the shared household; only breach of a protection order is criminal
16 to 18 may be tried as adults for heinous offences after a Board assessment
Presumption of severe stress on an attempted suicide, and advance directives

topics.why: Time limits and pecuniary limits are the mechanical marks here. The conceptual question is which Act is civil and which criminal — the Domestic Violence Act catches people out every year.

topics.title: Indra Sawhney (1992): reservation, the creamy layer and the 50% ceiling
topics.hook: The Mandal case. Nine judges, 27% for other backward classes upheld, promotions excluded, and a ceiling that Parliament has since gone around twice.
topics.story:
The **Mandal Commission**, formally the Second Backward Classes Commission, was set up in 1979 under **B.P. Mandal** and reported in 1980. It identified 3,743 castes as socially and educationally backward, estimated them at 52% of the population, and recommended 27% reservation in central government jobs. The report sat unused until **V.P. Singh** announced implementation on 7 August 1990, triggering nationwide protests.

*Indra Sawhney v. Union of India* (1992) was decided by **nine judges, 6-3**. The holdings:

- **27% reservation for OBCs in public employment is valid** under Article 16(4). Caste can be a starting point for identifying a backward class, provided backwardness is established.
- The **creamy layer** among OBCs must be excluded. This is the most examined element. The Court directed the government to fix criteria, done by the Ram Nandan Committee in 1993.
- Total reservation must not ordinarily exceed **50%**, except in extraordinary situations.
- **No reservation in promotions.** Parliament overturned this with the 77th Amendment (1995), inserting Article 16(4A), followed by the 81st (2000, carry-forward of backlog vacancies under 16(4B)), 82nd (2000, relaxation in qualifying marks) and 85th (2001, consequential seniority).
- An additional 10% reservation for economically backward sections not covered by 16(4), proposed by the government, was struck down: economic criteria alone cannot found a backward class.

That last holding is why the **103rd Amendment (2019)**, giving 10% to economically weaker sections through new clauses 15(6) and 16(6), needed a constitutional amendment. It was upheld 3-2 in *Janhit Abhiyan* (2022), the majority holding that the 50% ceiling is not inflexible and that EWS reservation, being outside 16(4), does not breach the basic structure. *M. Nagaraj* (2006) and *Jarnail Singh* (2018) held that the creamy layer principle applies to Scheduled Castes and Tribes in promotions too.

Mandal Commission, set up 1979, reported 1980, chaired by B.P. Mandal

No reservation, later reversed by the 77th Amendment, 1995

topics.why: Reservation passages are common and always turn on three numbers: 27, 50 and 10. The creamy layer question is the standard second-order test.

topics.title: Navtej Singh Johar (2018) and the dismantling of Victorian morality
topics.hook: Section 377 was drafted by Macaulay in 1860 and read down in 2018 by five judges who described the earlier decision restoring it as a mistake the Court had to correct.
topics.story:
**Section 377 of the Indian Penal Code** punished "carnal intercourse against the order of nature". It was part of Macaulay's draft code, enacted in 1860, and modelled on the English Buggery Act of 1533.

The litigation ran in three stages. In **Naz Foundation v. NCT of Delhi (2009)** the Delhi High Court read down section 377 to exclude consensual acts between adults in private, holding it violated Articles 14, 15 and 21. In **Suresh Kumar Koushal (2013)** a two-judge bench of the Supreme Court reversed that, saying only a "minuscule fraction" of the population was affected and that it was for Parliament to change the law. In **Navtej Singh Johar v. Union of India (6 September 2018)** a five-judge bench unanimously overruled Koushal and read down section 377 to decriminalise consensual sexual acts between adults. Chief Justice Dipak Misra, and Justices Nariman, Chandrachud and Indu Malhotra each wrote separately. Justice Malhotra's line that history owes an apology to members of the community is widely quoted.

The reasoning came directly from *Puttaswamy* (2017), which had recognised privacy including decisional autonomy and sexual orientation. The Court used **manifest arbitrariness** under Article 14, non-discrimination on grounds of sex under Article 15 read to include sexual orientation, and dignity under Article 21. Section 377 survives for non-consensual acts and acts with minors and animals; the new **Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita 2023** omits the provision entirely, which has left a gap regarding non-consensual acts between adult men.

The same bench season produced **Joseph Shine v. Union of India (2018)**, striking down section 497 IPC on adultery as a violation of Articles 14, 15 and 21, on the ground that it treated a wife as her husband's property and denied women agency. Read together with **Shakti Vahini** and **Shafin Jahan** on choice in marriage, and **Common Cause** on dignity in dying, 2018 was the year the Court applied Puttaswamy across the board.

*Supriyo v. Union of India* (2023) declined to recognise same-sex marriage, holding by 3-2 that this is for Parliament, while directing the government to form a committee on the rights of queer couples.

facts.k: High Court judgment restored in effect

facts.v: Joseph Shine v. Union of India, 2018, struck down section 497
Supriyo v. Union of India, 2023, declined 3-2

topics.title: Contract, tort and crime: the principles legal reasoning runs on
topics.hook: A legal reasoning question gives you the rule. What it tests is whether you will apply the rule you were given rather than the one you half remember.
topics.story:
**Contract.** The **Indian Contract Act, 1872** makes an agreement enforceable when there is offer and acceptance, lawful consideration, capacity, free consent and a lawful object. An **offer** must be distinguished from an **invitation to treat**: goods in a shop window invite offers, they do not make one. Acceptance must be **absolute and unqualified**; a counter-offer destroys the original. Consideration must move at the promisor's desire but **need not be adequate**, and under Indian law, unlike English, it may move from a third party. Consent is not free if obtained by **coercion, undue influence, fraud, misrepresentation or mistake**; the first four make the contract **voidable** at the option of the aggrieved party, while a bilateral mistake of fact makes it **void**. A minor's agreement is **void ab initio**, settled in **Mohori Bibee v. Dharmodas Ghose (1903)**. An agreement in restraint of trade, of marriage, or of legal proceedings is void. **Frustration** under Section 56 discharges a contract when performance becomes impossible or unlawful after it is made.

**Tort** is judge-made and uncodified in India. Liability generally requires a duty of care, its breach, and damage caused by the breach; **Donoghue v. Stevenson (1932)** is the source of the neighbour principle. **Vicarious liability** makes an employer answerable for an employee's tort committed in the course of employment. **Strict liability** under **Rylands v. Fletcher** applies to the escape of a dangerous thing brought onto land in a non-natural use, subject to exceptions. India went further in **M.C. Mehta v. Union of India (1987)**, the oleum gas leak case, and created **absolute liability** for enterprises in hazardous activity, with no exceptions at all, a rule later written into the Public Liability Insurance Act. Defences include **volenti non fit injuria**, consent to the risk, and contributory negligence.

**Criminal law.** An offence generally needs **actus reus**, the guilty act, and **mens rea**, the guilty mind, unless the statute creates strict liability. The general exceptions in the **Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita** cover mistake of fact, judicial acts, accident, necessity, infancy below seven and conditionally below twelve, unsoundness of mind, intoxication, consent, and **private defence**, which extends to causing death only in listed situations and must be proportionate.

facts.v: Offer, acceptance, consideration, capacity, free consent, lawful object
Displayed goods invite offers rather than making one
Need not be adequate; in India it may move from a third party
Coercion, undue influence, fraud and misrepresentation make a contract voidable; bilateral mistake makes it void
Void ab initio, from Mohori Bibee v. Dharmodas Ghose, 1903
Duty, breach, damage; the neighbour principle from Donoghue v. Stevenson, 1932
M.C. Mehta, 1987; no exceptions, unlike Rylands v. Fletcher
Actus reus and mens rea, unless the statute imposes strict liability

topics.why: In legal reasoning the passage supplies the principle and the facts, and marks are lost by importing outside knowledge. Learn these to recognise the structure, then answer only on what the passage gives you.

topics.title: The three new criminal laws that replaced the IPC, CrPC and Evidence Act
topics.hook: From 1 July 2024 India stopped prosecuting under an 1860 code. The names, the dates and what replaced what are guaranteed exam material.
topics.story:
Three statutes passed in December 2023 and brought into force on **1 July 2024** replaced the colonial criminal law framework:

- **Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023** replaces the **Indian Penal Code, 1860**. 358 sections against the IPC's 511.
- **Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023** replaces the **Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973**. 531 sections.
- **Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023** replaces the **Indian Evidence Act, 1872**. 170 sections.

The Union Home Minister **Amit Shah** introduced them; they were referred to the Standing Committee on Home Affairs and passed in the winter session while a large number of opposition members were suspended.

What changed substantively:

**Sedition, section 124A IPC, is gone.** In its place section 152 of the BNS creates the offence of "acts endangering the sovereignty, unity and integrity of India", covering secession, armed rebellion and subversive activities. Critics argue the new provision is broader than what it replaced. Sedition had been kept in abeyance by the Supreme Court in *S.G. Vombatkere* (2022) pending review of *Kedar Nath Singh* (1962), which had upheld it while confining it to incitement to violence.

**Terrorism enters the general criminal law.** Section 113 BNS defines a terrorist act, previously only in the UAPA.

**Mob lynching** becomes a distinct offence, punishable by death or life imprisonment where a group of five or more kills on grounds of race, caste, community, sex, language or personal belief.

**Community service** appears as a punishment for the first time. **Zero FIR** and electronic FIR are given statutory form, as is mandatory videography of search and seizure. Timelines are fixed: judgment within 45 days of the end of trial, charges framed within 60 days of the first hearing.

**Adultery and section 377 are not carried over**, following *Joseph Shine* and *Navtej Johar*. **Section 498A** on cruelty to a married woman survives as section 85 BNS.

facts.v: Section 124A IPC repealed; section 152 BNS covers acts endangering sovereignty

topics.why: Expect a passage on the new codes, and questions matching each new Act to the colonial statute it replaced. The sedition change is the most likely single question.

topics.title: Doctrines and maxims a law entrance expects you to know
topics.hook: Fifteen terms that turn up in legal reasoning passages, in questions on judgments, and in the reading comprehension section without warning.
topics.story:
**Constitutional doctrines.** *Basic structure*: Parliament may amend but not destroy the Constitution's identity. *Pith and substance*: a law is judged by its true nature, so incidental encroachment on another legislative list does not void it. *Colourable legislation*: what cannot be done directly cannot be done indirectly. *Eclipse*: a pre-Constitution law inconsistent with a Fundamental Right is dormant, not dead, and revives if the inconsistency is removed. *Severability*: only the offending portion is struck down if separable. *Harmonious construction*: conflicting provisions are read so that both are given effect. *Prospective overruling*: a new interpretation applies only to future cases, used in *Golaknath*. *Doctrine of repugnancy*: Article 254, Union law prevails on Concurrent subjects.

**Procedural terms.** *Locus standi*: standing to sue, relaxed by PIL. *Res judicata*: a matter already decided between the same parties cannot be relitigated. *Sub judice*: pending before a court. *Stare decisis*: stand by decided matters; precedent binds. *Obiter dicta*: things said in passing, persuasive but not binding. *Ratio decidendi*: the reason for the decision, which is the binding part. *Amicus curiae*: friend of the court, appointed to assist. *Suo motu*: on the court's own motion. *Ex parte*: a decision made in the absence of one party. *Caveat*: a notice asking that no order be passed without hearing the person who filed it.

**Maxims of substance.** *Audi alteram partem*: hear the other side. *Nemo judex in causa sua*: no one may judge their own cause. Together these make up natural justice. *Actus non facit reum nisi mens sit rea*: an act does not make a person guilty unless the mind is guilty, the basis of criminal intent. *Ignorantia juris non excusat*: ignorance of the law is no excuse. *Ubi jus ibi remedium*: where there is a right there is a remedy. *Volenti non fit injuria*: no injury is done to one who consents, a tort defence. *Res ipsa loquitur*: the thing speaks for itself, shifting the burden in negligence. *Damnum sine injuria*: loss without legal injury, which is not actionable. *Injuria sine damno*: legal injury without loss, which is actionable, as in *Ashby v. White*.

facts.k: No one a judge in his own cause
Loss without legal injury, not actionable

topics.why: Legal reasoning passages use these terms without defining them, and the GK section asks for the meaning directly. The pair most often confused is damnum sine injuria against injuria sine damno.

passages.title: The Mandal case
passages.passage:
A commission appointed in 1979 to identify socially and educationally backward classes reported the following year that such groups made up a little over half the population, and recommended that twenty-seven per cent of central government posts be reserved for them. The report was shelved for a decade. When a coalition government announced in August 1990 that it would implement the recommendation, the announcement set off protests across northern India and the government fell within months.

The litigation that followed was heard by nine judges. The Court upheld the twenty-seven per cent reservation, holding that caste could serve as the starting point for identifying a backward class provided social and educational backwardness was actually established. It then imposed three limits. The better-off members of a backward class, those who had already escaped the disadvantages that justified the classification, were to be excluded from its benefits. Total reservation was not ordinarily to exceed half of the available posts, since reservation is an exception to the general rule of equality of opportunity and an exception cannot swallow the rule. And reservation was to apply to appointments, not to promotions.

The government had also proposed a further ten per cent for sections that were poor but not socially backward. The Court struck this down, holding that economic criteria alone could not identify a backward class within the meaning of the relevant clause.

Parliament responded to two of these holdings. A constitutional amendment in 1995 restored reservation in promotions for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes; three further amendments over the next six years dealt with backlog vacancies, qualifying marks and consequential seniority. Almost thirty years after the judgment, another amendment created a ten per cent quota on purely economic grounds by placing it in new clauses outside the provision the Court had interpreted. A five-judge bench upheld it by a majority of three to two.

questions.q: The commission described in the first paragraph is the:
questions.explain: The Mandal Commission, the Second Backward Classes Commission, appointed 1979 under B.P. Mandal and reporting in 1980. Kalelkar chaired the first such commission in 1953; Sarkaria and Punchhi dealt with centre-state relations.

questions.q: The exclusion described in the second paragraph is known as the:
questions.explain: The creamy layer. Criteria were fixed by the Ram Nandan Committee in 1993. Carry-forward and consequential seniority relate to promotion amendments that came later.

questions.q: Why was the government’s proposed ten per cent quota struck down in 1992?
options: It breached the fifty per cent ceiling
Economic criteria alone cannot identify a backward class under Article 16(4)
It had not been recommended by any commission
It applied to promotions rather than appointments
questions.explain: The Court held that backwardness under Article 16(4) is social and educational, so poverty alone could not found a backward class. This is precisely why the 2019 EWS quota needed a constitutional amendment rather than an executive order.

questions.q: The 1995 amendment referred to in the final paragraph inserted which provision?
questions.explain: The 77th Amendment inserted Article 16(4A), permitting reservation in promotion for Scheduled Castes and Tribes. 16(4B) came with the 81st Amendment on backlog vacancies; 15(6) came with the 103rd for EWS.

questions.q: The amendment upheld three to two by a five-judge bench is the:
questions.explain: The 103rd Amendment of 2019, creating the ten per cent EWS quota, upheld in Janhit Abhiyan (2022). The 102nd gave the NCBC constitutional status; the 106th is the women’s reservation amendment.

passages.title: Privacy as a right
passages.passage:
The question reached a bench of nine judges by an awkward route. A challenge to the government's biometric identification programme had been running for years, and the Attorney General met it with an argument that went to the root: the Constitution contains no right to privacy at all, and two old benches had said so. One was an eight-judge bench from 1954 that had refused to read an American-style protection against search and seizure into Indian law. The other was a six-judge bench from 1962 that had struck down night-time police visits to a suspect's house while denying that privacy as such was a guaranteed right. Since no later bench had been large enough to overrule them, the point had to be settled before the main case could proceed.

The 2017 answer was unanimous in result and split into six opinions in reasoning. Privacy was held to be intrinsic to the life and personal liberty protected by Article 21, and to run through the other freedoms in Part III as well. The Court declined to treat it as a single narrow interest, describing it instead as covering bodily integrity, informational self-determination and the freedom to make personal choices about family, marriage and sexual orientation. The two earlier decisions were expressly overruled to the extent they held otherwise.

The right was not made absolute. Any state intrusion has to satisfy a test with three limbs, later stated as four: there must be a law, that law must serve a legitimate state aim, the means must be rationally connected and no more restrictive than necessary, and there must be procedural safeguards against abuse. That test has since been used to strike at colonial-era criminal law and to assess data collection by the state.

One passage in the judgment did unfinished work. It criticised a 2013 decision that had restored the criminal ban on consensual same-sex relations, on the ground that the size of the affected group cannot determine whether a right exists. A five-judge bench acted on that reasoning the following year.

questions.q: The nine-judge decision described is:
options: K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India
Kharak Singh v. State of U.P.
Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India
questions.explain: K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017), decided by nine judges and reported as the privacy judgment.

questions.q: The two earlier decisions overruled were of benches numbering:
questions.explain: M.P. Sharma (1954) was eight judges and Kharak Singh (1962) was six, which is why a nine-judge bench was needed to overrule them.

questions.q: The right to privacy was located primarily in:
questions.explain: Article 21, as intrinsic to life and personal liberty, though the Court held privacy also runs through other Part III freedoms.

questions.q: The test the passage describes for permissible intrusion is known as:
questions.explain: Proportionality: legality, legitimate aim, necessity and least restrictive means, and procedural safeguards.

questions.q: The 2013 decision criticised in the judgment was acted upon by a five-judge bench in:
questions.explain: Navtej Singh Johar v. Union of India (2018) read down Section 377 IPC, overruling Suresh Kumar Koushal (2013).

passages.title: The rule India wrote for itself
passages.passage:
The English rule came out of a Lancashire case in 1868. A mill owner built a reservoir; water escaped through disused shafts into a neighbouring colliery and flooded it. There was no negligence, because the contractors had been competent and the shafts unknown. The court held nonetheless that a person who brings onto land and keeps there anything likely to do mischief if it escapes, in a use of land that is not natural, must keep it at his peril and is answerable for all the damage that follows. The rule was strict but not unqualified: it did not apply where the escape was caused by an act of God, by the act of a stranger, by the plaintiff's own fault, or with the plaintiff's consent, nor where the thing was kept under statutory authority.

A little over a hundred years later, weeks after a gas leak in central India had killed thousands, oleum gas escaped from a plant in Delhi and injured several people. The Supreme Court, hearing a petition about the plant, took the opportunity to consider whether the old rule was adequate for an economy that had industrialised on a scale the Lancashire judges never contemplated.

It held that it was not. Where an enterprise is engaged in a hazardous or inherently dangerous activity and harm results, the enterprise is strictly and absolutely liable to compensate all those affected, and the liability is not subject to any of the exceptions to the older rule. The reasoning was that such an enterprise owes an absolute and non-delegable duty to the community, that it alone can guard against the hazard, and that the cost of an accident should be treated as an overhead of the activity itself. The court added that compensation must be correlated to the magnitude and capacity of the enterprise, so that it has a deterrent effect.

The rule has since been given statutory form for certain hazardous industries, with compulsory insurance and a no-fault relief scheme, and the National Green Tribunal was later empowered to apply it directly.

questions.q: The 1868 English case referred to is:
questions.explain: Rylands v. Fletcher, the source of the strict liability rule.

questions.q: Under the English rule, liability did NOT arise where the escape was caused by:
options: The escape of a dangerous thing
questions.explain: Act of a stranger is one of the recognised exceptions, along with act of God, plaintiff's fault and consent.

questions.q: The Indian case described in the third paragraph established:
questions.explain: M.C. Mehta v. Union of India (1987) laid down absolute liability.

questions.q: On the passage, the essential difference between the two rules is that the Indian one:
questions.explain: The passage says the liability is not subject to any of the exceptions to the older rule.

questions.q: The court said compensation should be correlated to:
options: The magnitude and capacity of the enterprise
The market value of the property
questions.explain: So that the award has a deterrent effect on an enterprise of that size.

passages.title: A right built out of another right
passages.passage:
Before the statute there was a case. Villagers in Rajasthan demanding to see muster rolls and bills for public works in the early 1990s built a campaign around a slogan about the right to know being the right to live, and the movement they started supplied both the political pressure and the draft. The courts had already provided the constitutional footing, reading a right to know into the freedom of speech and expression on the reasoning that a citizen cannot form or express an opinion on public affairs without access to the facts about them.

The Act that followed in 2005 is procedural rather than declaratory. Every public authority must designate an officer to receive requests. The officer must dispose of a request within thirty days, and within forty-eight hours where the information concerns the life or liberty of a person. Refusal must state reasons and the appeal route. A first appeal lies within the authority; a second lies to a commission at the centre or in the state, which may impose a penalty on the officer personally for a refusal without reasonable cause.

The exemptions are listed and closed. They cover sovereignty and integrity, information forbidden by a court, breach of parliamentary privilege, commercial confidence and trade secrets, information held in a fiduciary relationship, information received in confidence from a foreign government, information endangering life or safety, information impeding investigation, cabinet papers until a decision is taken, and personal information bearing no relationship to public activity. Almost all of them yield where the public interest in disclosure outweighs the harm.

Two later changes narrowed it. An amendment in 2019 moved the tenure and salary of the commissioners out of the statute and into rules made by the central government, which critics said converted a fixed term into a favour. And the data protection statute of 2023 amended the personal information exemption to remove the public interest override that had until then allowed disclosure of, for instance, the assets of a public servant.

questions.q: The constitutional footing for the right was found in:
questions.explain: The right to know was read into the freedom of speech and expression.

questions.q: The ordinary time limit for disposing of a request is:
questions.explain: Thirty days, reduced to forty-eight hours where life or liberty is concerned.

questions.q: A penalty for refusal without reasonable cause may be imposed on:
questions.explain: The commission may penalise the Public Information Officer personally.

questions.q: On the passage, the 2019 amendment was criticised because it:
options: Moved commissioners' tenure and salary into executive rules
questions.explain: Moving a statutory term into rules made by the government was said to convert a fixed term into a favour.

questions.q: The 2023 change to the personal information exemption:
options: Applied it only to private bodies
questions.explain: The DPDP Act removed the override that had permitted disclosure in the public interest.

passages.title: The limit nobody wrote down
passages.passage:
The text is not ambiguous. One article says Parliament may in exercise of its constituent power amend by way of addition, variation or repeal any provision of this Constitution in accordance with the procedure laid down. Read plainly, that permits anything, including the repeal of the chapter on fundamental rights.

The courts arrived at the opposite conclusion in stages, and reversed themselves twice on the way. An early decision in 1951 held that an amendment was not law within the meaning of the article that voids laws inconsistent with fundamental rights, so amendments could not be tested against those rights. A bench of eleven judges in 1967 reversed that, holding that an amendment was law after all and that fundamental rights were therefore beyond amendment altogether, though it applied the ruling only to the future. Parliament answered with an amendment declaring that nothing in the amending article would be subject to the voiding provision and that Parliament's power extended to any provision.

Thirteen judges then sat for sixty-eight days in 1972 and 1973. The petitioner was the head of a religious institution in Kerala challenging land legislation; the case became the vehicle for the constitutional question. The judgment runs to more than seven hundred pages and eleven opinions, and the operative order was signed by nine judges and disputed almost immediately. What it held was that the amending power is wide but not unlimited: Parliament may amend any article, including the chapter on rights, but may not damage or destroy the essential features of the document. Which features those are was deliberately not exhaustively listed.

The doctrine has since been used sparingly and decisively. It struck down a clause inserted during the Emergency that had placed a particular election beyond judicial review. It struck down provisions giving Parliament unlimited amending power and immunising certain laws from challenge, in a judgment holding that the balance between rights and directive principles is itself essential. And it struck down a commission for judicial appointments in 2015. Features identified along the way include judicial review, secularism, federalism, free and fair elections, separation of powers and the rule of law.

questions.q: The article permitting amendment is:
questions.explain: Article 368 confers the amending power and prescribes the procedure.

questions.q: The 1967 decision holding fundamental rights unamendable is:
questions.explain: Golaknath v. State of Punjab, decided by eleven judges, applied prospectively.

questions.q: The thirteen-judge case was decided in:
questions.explain: Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala, 1973.

questions.q: On the passage, what did that judgment hold?
options: Any article may be amended but essential features may not be destroyed
Only fundamental rights may be amended
Amendments require ratification by all states
questions.explain: The amending power is plenary in reach but limited by the basic structure.

questions.q: The judgment holding that the balance between rights and directive principles is itself a basic feature is:
questions.explain: Minerva Mills v. Union of India (1980) struck down clauses inserted by the 42nd Amendment.

passages.title: A smoke ball and a hundred pounds
passages.passage:
A company advertised a device in the winter of 1891, claiming it prevented influenza, and offered a reward of a hundred pounds to any person who contracted the disease after using it three times daily for two weeks as directed. The advertisement added that a thousand pounds had been deposited with a named bank to show sincerity in the matter. A woman bought one, used it as directed, and caught influenza. She sued for the hundred pounds.

The company's defences were a catalogue of everything a first-year student is later taught. The advertisement was mere puff, not intended to create legal relations. It was an offer to the whole world and one cannot contract with the world. There had been no communication of acceptance. There was no consideration moving from her. And the terms were too vague to enforce, since no period was specified within which the illness had to occur.

The court rejected each. The deposit with the bank answered the argument about puff; a person who says he has set money aside to meet claims is not joking. An offer may indeed be made to the world at large, and it ripens into a contract with whoever comes forward and performs the conditions. In an offer of this kind, notification of acceptance before performance is dispensed with, because the offeror by implication indicates that performance is enough. Consideration was found in two places: the inconvenience of using the device as prescribed, and the benefit to the company of the sales the advertisement generated. And the vagueness objection failed because the promise could be given a reasonable construction.

The case supplies the standard illustration of a unilateral contract and of the line between an offer and an invitation to treat. Goods in a shop window, price lists and auction notices invite offers; an advertisement promising a reward on defined terms makes one.

questions.q: The advertisement was held to be:
options: An offer to the world at large
questions.explain: An offer capable of acceptance by anyone who performed the conditions.

questions.q: On the passage, communication of acceptance was unnecessary because:
options: The company waived it in writing
Performance of the conditions was itself acceptance
The plaintiff had paid for the device
The offer was made in a newspaper
questions.explain: In a unilateral offer the offeror impliedly dispenses with prior notification.

questions.q: The deposit with the bank was relevant to the defence of:
questions.explain: It showed an intention to be legally bound.

questions.q: Consideration was found in:
options: The inconvenience of use and the benefit of increased sales
questions.explain: The court identified both a detriment to the plaintiff and a benefit to the company.

questions.q: Which of the following is, on the passage, an invitation to treat?
options: A reward advertisement on defined terms
Goods displayed in a shop window
questions.explain: Displayed goods and price lists invite offers rather than making them.
